blocks.text: A danfo driver on the Ikorodu road charges different fares across a morning: ₦200, ₦250, ₦200, ₦300, ₦200. What is a typical fare? The mean, the median and the mode will each give an answer, and they will not always agree. Choosing the right average is as important as calculating it.

blocks.markdown:
There are three common averages.

The **mean** of raw data is $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n}$. If the same values repeat, group them first and use $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$.

The **median** is the middle value once the data are ordered. For an odd $n$, it is the $\frac{n+1}{2}$th value. For an even $n$, it is the average of the $\frac{n}{2}$th and $\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right)$th values.

The **mode** is the value that occurs most often. For grouped data, the class with the highest frequency is the **modal class**.

blocks.title: Mean of grouped data
blocks.text: When data are grouped into classes, every value in a class is represented by the class midpoint $x_m$. The estimated mean is $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum f x_m}{\sum f}$. It is an estimate because we no longer know the original list.

blocks.caption: Which formula to reach for depends on how the data are presented

blocks.title: Mean of ungrouped frequency data
blocks.prompt: The marks of ten students are 4, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9, 10. Find the mean.

blocks.markdown:
### Even $n$ and the median

For the ordered set $4, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18$ there are six values. The median is not $9$ and it is not $11$ — it is their average:

$\text{median} = \frac{9 + 11}{2} = 10$.

On a frequency table, find $n = \sum f$, then walk down the cumulative-frequency column until you pass the median position. The score in that row is the median.

blocks.title: Estimated mean from grouped classes
blocks.prompt: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30 have frequencies 3, 5 and 2. Estimate the mean using midpoints.

steps.text: Write the midpoints of each class.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: The midpoint of $10$–$20$ is $15$, not $10$ and not $20$. Using a class limit in place of $x_m$ is the fastest way to lose the grouped-mean question. For an even count, averaging the two middle values is compulsory — taking just one of them is a mid-range error, not the median.

points: Raw mean: $\bar{x} = \sum x / n$. Frequency mean: $\bar{x} = \sum fx / \sum f$.
For even $n$, the median is the average of the $n/2$th and $(n/2 + 1)$th values.
The mode is the most frequent value; the modal class is the class with the largest frequency.
Grouped mean uses midpoints: $\bar{x} = \sum f x_m / \sum f$.
The mean uses every value, the median is resistant to extremes, and the mode names the most typical category.
